title: Principles of Microeconomics in Marginal Falls
subtitle: One town. Five acts. Sixteen modules.
author: Promit K. Chaudhuri

acts.title: Building the Stage
acts.question: What can a town do with limited resources?
acts.description: Establish the rules of Marginal Falls: scarcity forces choices, incentives shape behavior, and trade changes what the town can achieve.

acts.title: Casting the Buyers
acts.question: What do the citizens want, and what can they afford?
acts.description: Start with a citizen's choices. Utility and budgets lead to individual demand, market demand, and the responsiveness of buyers to price changes.

acts.title: Casting the Sellers
acts.question: How do local businesses decide what to produce?
acts.description: Go backstage at the bakery. Technology and input choices create costs; costs and prices shape output, supply, and sellers' responses.

acts.title: The Play Begins
acts.question: What happens when the town's plans meet?
acts.description: Bring buyers and sellers together. Study equilibrium and gains from exchange, then examine policy, market failures, and the market for labor.

acts.title: Different Stages
acts.question: How does the way firms compete change the outcome?
acts.description: Visit the farmers market, the corporate district, Main Street, and the boardroom to compare competition, market power, differentiation, and strategic interaction.

modules.title: Founding Marginal Falls
modules.story: Marginal Falls has ambitious plans for parks, homes, roads, and festivals, but limited land, time, and money. The founding decisions introduce the economic problem that runs through the course: choosing among desirable uses of scarce resources.
modules.question: When the mayor changes a rule, why might citizens respond differently from what the mayor intended?

modules.title: The Port of Marginal Falls
modules.story: The port opens, and the town must decide what to make and what to obtain through exchange. Comparing opportunity costs shows why a town can gain from trade even when its trading partner is more productive at making every good.
modules.question: If another town can produce both goods using fewer resources, can Marginal Falls still benefit from trading with it?

modules.title: Citizen Motivations
modules.story: Citizens want coffee, pastries, ferry rides, and answers to a mystery. The investigation activities turn a limited budget into a choice between competing uses of resources, connecting the value of one more purchase to the best affordable bundle.
modules.question: When is buying one more clue worthwhile, and how should a fixed investigation budget be divided?

modules.title: The Shopping List
modules.topic: Demand curves, market demand, and demand shifters
modules.story: The detective department now faces changing forensic prices. Repeating its choice at different prices produces a demand schedule. The same logic takes the course from a single citizen's shopping list to the town's market demand.
modules.question: Which changes move a citizen along a demand curve, and which changes create a new demand curve?

modules.title: Buyer Sensitivity
modules.story: A price increase does not affect every purchase equally. Sorting the town's goods by buyer responsiveness makes elasticity concrete and connects substitutes, time, and necessity to the effect of a price change on revenue.
modules.question: Why might buyers react strongly to a higher coffee price but only slightly to a higher price for an urgent purchase?

modules.title: Backstage at the Bakery
modules.story: Founders' Night brings a large order for bread, pastries, cakes, and snack boxes. Behind the counter, the bakery must combine workers and equipment. The production process connects additional workers to output and then to the cost of serving the town.
concepts: Fixed, variable, average, and marginal costs
modules.question: Why can an additional worker add less output when the bakery's equipment stays fixed?

modules.title: The Shopkeeper's Offer
modules.topic: Profit maximization and the supply curve
modules.story: The mayor announces a pastry price. Each seller must decide how much to produce at that price. Comparing the revenue and cost of additional output reveals how a firm's production choices become a supply curve.
modules.question: At a given market price, what tells the bakery whether producing one more pastry raises profit?

modules.title: Profit and Sensitivity
modules.story: The bakery has chosen its output, but how far can it expand when pastry prices rise? Capacity, the availability of inputs, and time determine how responsive sellers can be. The slide deck introduces this module as Seller Sensitivity.
modules.question: Why might the bakery respond little to a price increase tonight but much more over the next year?

modules.title: The Town Square
modules.story: The mayor steps back from announcing prices. Buyers arrive with demand plans and sellers arrive with supply plans. The town square shows how prices coordinate those plans and how shortages and surpluses put pressure on the market outcome.
modules.question: What happens when the posted price makes buyers want more pastries than sellers are willing to provide?

modules.title: Fair Play
modules.story: The town has a market price, but who gains from exchange? The Berry Vault introduces reservation values and surplus. Price controls and taxes then show how policies can change the distribution of gains and the number of mutually beneficial trades.
modules.question: How can a policy intended to help one group change both who gains and how much total surplus the town creates?

modules.title: Town Crisis
modules.story: A smoke complaint introduces a resident who is affected by a transaction without being a buyer or seller. The town must now distinguish private incentives from social costs and benefits, and ask how goods used collectively will be provided.
concepts: Private and social costs and benefits
modules.question: Can an exchange benefit its buyer and seller while imposing a cost on someone else in Marginal Falls?

modules.title: Hiring Hall
modules.story: The bakery receives another order and considers hiring. Workers are valuable because their production can be sold, so labor demand is derived from demand for the bakery's output. The hiring hall connects product markets to input prices and wages.
modules.question: How does greater demand for pastries affect the value of an additional bakery worker?

modules.title: The Farmers Market
modules.story: Many stalls sell comparable products, and no single stall controls the market price. The farmers market returns to output and profit decisions in a competitive setting and examines how entry and exit change the longer-run outcome.
modules.question: Why does a competitive stall take the market price as given even though it chooses its own output?

modules.title: The Corporate District
modules.story: River-Gate is the only seller of bridge passes for entry to Founders' Night. There is no nearby alternative. The corporate district uses this bottleneck to connect barriers to entry with market power, a downward-sloping demand curve, and the monopoly's output decision.
modules.question: Why must River-Gate consider the effect on its existing sales when deciding whether to sell another bridge pass?

modules.title: The Main Street
modules.story: Main Street has many businesses, but they are not identical. Moonlit Mocha can retain some customers after raising its price because people value its coffee, atmosphere, or location. Differentiation introduces market power alongside competition and entry.
modules.question: How can Moonlit Mocha have some market power while still facing many competitors?

modules.title: The Boardroom
modules.story: Two shuttle operators choose fares, and each operator's profit depends on its rival's decision. The boardroom introduces strategic interdependence: a sensible choice cannot be assessed without asking what the other firm will do.
modules.question: Why can the firms reach an outcome that neither would choose if they could jointly commit to fares?

games.title: Mayor's Dilemma
games.description: Choose policy incentives and examine how citizens respond when the rules change.

games.title: Riverside Choice
games.description: Allocate scarce riverfront land between parks and apartments and weigh trade-offs at the margin.

games.title: Port Ledger Game
games.description: Explore production choices and exchange at the port alongside the comparative-advantage module.

games.title: Marginal Falls Murder
games.description: Purchase clues and compare the benefit of more information with its cost.

games.title: Operation: Contingency Plan
games.description: Choose an investigation bundle under a fixed budget by comparing marginal conviction gains.

games.title: Operation: Contingency Plan — Demand
games.description: Reconsider the investigation bundle at changing forensic prices to construct demand.

games.title: Elasticity Jar Sort
games.description: Sort town goods by demand responsiveness using substitutes, urgency, and time.

games.title: The Block Party
games.description: Plan the town party and connect total output, marginal product, and costs.

games.title: Founders' Night Exchange
games.description: Trade pastry ingredients and examine how market prices coordinate buyers and sellers.

games.title: The Berry Vault
games.description: Use reservation values and market prices to discuss the gains from exchange.

games.title: Price Posting Market
games.description: Post storefront prices over successive rounds and observe competitive pressure.

games.title: Differentiate for Donations
games.description: Create a distinctive charity name and slogan and examine the role of differentiation.

games.title: The Starlight Shuttle War
games.description: Choose fares against a rival and identify best responses and a Nash equilibrium.
